newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds marked down, supply/inflation focus.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds marked down, supply/inflation focus.

text.p: Irish bond prices were marked down on Friday and failed to recoup losses later in the day as benign U.S. PPI data boosted afternoon overseas trade.
Dealers said inflation numbers, both domestic and in the U.S., will set the tone next week.

"For us it is the Irish February CPI on Thursday. We are expecting 2.0 percent Irish inflation," Riada economist Padhraic Garvey said. "I think the market should be reasonably happy with that if that is the case."
In January, Irish inflation was 1.9 percent and Garvey said that once the number stays close to 2.0 percent "... you could not really be unhappy considering how strong the economy is."
The other major domestic factor next week is the National Treasury Management Agency's 150 punt auction in the Treasury bond due 2006 on Tuesday.

"I think there will be a demand for it (the 10-year auction issue) but it may not be particularly large," one dealer said, adding that Irish 10-year paper was about 10 basis points cheaper than it had been relative to bunds since the last tap, which occurred in January.
Overseas, the dealer said the key focus will be U.S. CPI data which was likely to determine the tone for all markets.

"The U.S. CPI is really the main number and we are expecting a reasonably good figure. U.S. inflation is currently running at 3.0 percent and we would expect it to hold that level." Riada's Garvey said.
He said U.S. capacity utililisation numbers, released earlier, were "... a bit of a damp squid".
"They came in almost exactly as expected and didn't really move the market either way," Garvey said.

The numbers followed strong U.S. retail sales data on Thursday which resulted in the market falling away," a dealer said. "But prices at the wholesale level (released Friday) tumbled in February in the U.S. and that is the latest indication that inflationay pressures have been largely wrung out of the economy."
The U.S. Producer Price Index, on Friday, fell 0.4 percent after declining 0.3 percent in January. It was the first time since the autumn of 1994 that the index retreated two months in a row.

By 1545 GMT, the Irish 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was marginally down at 101.68 to yield 6.05 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 dropped 17 pence to 108.83 to yield 6.69 percent.
